Rhythm Notation from Du De: Note Values and Time Signatures

Chapter 4 of Hutchinson’s Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom for students who already read and write rhythm with MLT syllables: note-value names, dots and ties, time signatures and tuplets as new names for what they already chant.

This page goes with Chapter 4, Basics of Rhythm of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom.

You already know this. You move to macrobeats and microbeats, chant rhythm patterns on du de (usual duple) and du da di (usual triple) (Gordon 86, 105), and read and write those patterns. This chapter gives the textbook’s names for the symbols you already read. Gordon’s warning applies: a player who only knows the time-value names “resort[s] to counting”, and the tempo and meter suffer (Gordon 38). So keep chanting: the names are for talking about the notation, not for performing from it.

Press ▶ to hear an example. Click any heading to fold its section.

What you know → what the book calls it

You say (MLT) The book says (Hutchinson ch. 4)
macrobeat the beat (in simple meter); the dotted beat (in compound meter)
microbeat the division of the beat
du, de, du da di, ta note values: quarter, eighth, sixteenth …
an elongation (a note longer than a microbeat) a longer value, a dotted note, or a tie
usual duple / usual triple simple / compound meter (see Meter: Two Ways)
a triple division inside duple meter (usual combined) a triplet (a tuplet)
the measure signature the time signature

4.1 and 4.4 Time signatures and meter

The book reads the time signature as two numbers: how many beats in a bar, and what kind of note gets the beat. Read 4.1 · Read 4.4

The two systems sort meters differently, and this is the one place in the chapter where they disagree. The full comparison is on Meter: Two Ways to Sort Time Signatures. The short version:

  • Simple meter (2/4, 3/4, 4/4): each beat divides in 2. You chant it du de: usual duple.
  • Compound meter (6/8, 9/8, 12/8): each beat divides in 3. You chant it du da di: usual triple.
  • The book’s duple / triple / quadruple counts beats in a bar. Your duple / triple names how each beat divides. So 6/8 is “compound duple” in the book and “usual triple” to you (Gordon 176).

4.2 Note values: naming what you chant

Here is one bar of usual duple in 2/4 and one of usual triple in 6/8, with your syllables under the notes. Read 4.2

In 2/4 you chant The book’s name US / UK name
du (a macrobeat) quarter note, the beat quarter / crotchet
du de (two microbeats) two eighth notes eighth / quaver
du ta de ta four sixteenth notes sixteenth / semiquaver
du held through two macrobeats half note half / minim
In 6/8 you chant The book’s name
du (a macrobeat) dotted quarter note, the beat
du da di three eighth notes
du … di (long-short) quarter then eighth
du held through two macrobeats dotted half note

The thing to notice: in 2/4 the macrobeat is a quarter note; in 6/8 it is a dotted quarter. That is why compound meters need dots: a plain note can’t be split evenly into three.

4.3 Dots and ties: names for elongations

A note longer than a microbeat is an elongation. You already read them. The book has two ways to write them. Read 4.3

  • A dot adds half the note’s value. In 2/4, a dotted quarter + eighth is the pattern you chant du — de, held through the first microbeat of the next beat.
  • A tie joins two notes into one sound. Use it when the sound crosses a barline, or a beat the reader needs to see.

4.5 Tuplets: usual combined

When a duple beat is split into three, you chant du da di inside usual duple: Gordon calls the mix usual combined (Gordon 175–176). The book writes it as a triplet, with a 3 over the notes. Read 4.5

4.6 Writing rhythms the reader can audiate

The book’s list of common errors is mostly one rule: show the beat. Beam notes so each macrobeat’s microbeats are grouped together, and tie across the middle of the bar rather than hiding it inside one long note. If you can see where each du falls, you can chant it at sight. Read 4.6

Bridging: from syllables to names

  1. Chant first. Chant the pattern on du de or du da di, moving to the macrobeats.
  2. Find du. Every du is a macrobeat. Say which note value it is: quarter in 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4; dotted quarter in 6/8.
  3. Name the rest from du. A de is half of it, a ta a quarter of it. A note held through a du is an elongation: name it as a longer note, a dot or a tie.
  4. Go the other way. Given “write four eighths and a half note in 2/4”, chant it first (du de du de | du), then write it.

Check yourself

  1. In 3/4, what note value is du?
  2. In 6/8, you chant du da di. What are the three notes called?
  3. In 2/4, you chant du ta de ta. Name the notes.
  4. What does the book call usual combined meter’s triple division inside a duple beat?
  5. Why does 6/8 need a dotted quarter for its beat?
TipAnswers
  1. A quarter note.
  2. Eighth notes.
  3. Four sixteenth notes.
  4. A triplet (a kind of tuplet).
  5. Its beat divides in three eighths; only a dotted quarter lasts three eighths.

Practise reading and chanting with Rhythm Patterns. Related: Major Scales and Key Signatures.

Works Cited

Gordon, Edwin E. Learning Sequences in Music: A Contemporary Music Learning Theory. 2012 ed., GIA Publications, 2012. Skill learning sequence: partial synthesis (pp. 111–117), the verbal association warning (p. 108), generalization-aural/oral and -verbal (pp. 131–133); same is easier to hear than different (p. 219); tonal and rhythm patterns kept apart (p. 223); rhythm patterns chanted with vocal inflection like speech (p. 101); macrobeats stressed, not accented, and approached with a decrescendo, expression found between macrobeats, anacruses given special attention, weight and flow, displaced energy in rests and long durations (pp. 187–190).; Theory Concepts pages: Keyality versus key signature (p. xiii); tonality “best refers to what is usually called a mode,” the eight tonalities (p. 149); movable-do with la-based minor and the rhythm syllables du de, du da di (p. 105); resting tone and tonic, a tonality in any keyality (p. 150); unitonal and multitonal music (pp. 152, 157); usual duple, triple and combined meter (pp. 175–176); no direct relation between measure signatures and meter, 6/8 as “duple compound” called inaccurate (p. 176); accents and microbeat divisions do not make meter (pp. 176–177); unusual meter, paired and unpaired, intact, macrobeats versus microbeats establishing meter (pp. 179–180); key signatures as do signatures, one signature for many tonalities (pp. 155–156); rhythm syllables by beat function (p. 86); time-value names lead to counting (p. 38); writing tonal patterns from a familiar do signature (p. 125).; Course pages (glossary, enrichment): audiation defined and compared with imitation (Introduction; pp. 3, 9); notation as a window (p. 8); patterns as units of meaning (pp. 99–100); the aural/oral level and the pause (pp. 101–102); discrimination and inference learning, theory delayed (p. 106); levels of the skill learning sequence (from pp. 111, 117, 126, 129, 136, 141); stepwise and bridging movement, Table 17 (pp. 230–231).

Hutchinson, Robert. “Basics of Rhythm.” Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom, University of Puget Sound, musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/BasicsOfRhythm.html. Chapter 4: time signature, durational symbols, dots and ties, meter, tuplets, common notation errors.

Hutchinson, Robert. “Meter.” Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom, University of Puget Sound, musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/meter.html. Simple and compound, duple, triple and quadruple, with example signatures.
